opus-5.5.text:
Well, I mean, I like the idea in principle. I've known Steve for a long time, and the notion that you'd have hardware and software that's formally verified, where you can mathematically prove certain safety properties hold, that's a beautiful vision. And in the long run, I think something like that may well be part of how we get a robust, secure computing infrastructure.

But the problem is just the sheer gap between where we are and where that would need to be. Look at the current state of formal verification. We can prove properties of fairly small, carefully designed systems: a microkernel like seL4, some cryptographic protocols, certain compilers. That took enormous expert effort for systems that are tiny compared to the whole stack running the world's computing. Now think about rebuilding the entire technological infrastructure, chips, operating systems, networks, the whole global internet, on provably secure foundations. That's not a five-year project. Even with AI theorem provers getting much better, which they are, you're talking about ripping out and replacing a massive legacy installed base that's deeply entangled with the economy.

And then there's the specification problem, which is maybe even deeper. To prove something is safe, you have to formally specify what "safe" means. For a memory-safety property, fine. But for "this AI system won't do something harmful in the real world," what's the formal spec? The real world is messy and open-ended, and you can't write a complete mathematical model of human values or of all the physical consequences of an action. So you prove things relative to a model, and the model is always an approximation.

There's also the political economy angle. Who's going to coordinate this? You'd need governments, big tech companies, chip manufacturers, all agreeing to adopt this infrastructure and lock out unverified systems. Meanwhile the competitive race in AI is going full speed. Nobody's going to pause deploying powerful models for ten or twenty years while we rebuild everything with proofs attached.

So my view is it's a worthwhile research direction, and pieces of it, like verified components in critical systems, are valuable and we should push on them. But as a near-term solution to the AGI safety problem, I just don't see it. By the time you could realistically deploy that kind of infrastructure at scale, we'll likely already have AGI, and probably the AGI will be helping design whatever infrastructure we end up with. So I think we need approaches that work in the messy, unverified world we actually have: decentralization, open development, and trying to make sure the early AGIs have good values and are developed in a beneficial way, rather than counting on a mathematical cage that won't be built in time.

r001.rationale: The response cites expert effort and the cost of replacing legacy systems, but does not identify computational overhead from security measures.

r002.rationale: It does not mention quantum computing or homomorphic encryption.

r003.rationale: It says current verification covers only small, carefully designed systems and contrasts them with the entire global technology stack, describing that gap as an obstacle to near-term deployment.

r004.rationale: It mentions coordination and the fast AI race, but does not explain that a country’s unilateral adoption would be undermined by countries that skip the measures.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I want to be clear first that I think Steve and Max are pointing at something real and important. If you could actually get provably safe AI systems running on provably secure hardware and software, with formal guarantees all the way down the stack, that would be wonderful. I just don't think it's a near-term thing, and I'm skeptical about treating it as something we can rely on in the timeframe when AGI is likely to arrive.

Part of my skepticism comes from history. Formal verification has been a research area for many decades. We have had people working on verified operating system kernels, verified compilers, verified hardware, and the results are real but they are tiny compared to the actual software ecosystem. Verifying seL4 took something like a decade of effort for a kernel of maybe ten thousand lines. Meanwhile the software that actually runs the world is hundreds of millions of lines of C and C++ and Python and JavaScript, mostly undocumented, mostly written under commercial pressure. The gap between what we can verify and what we actually deploy has been widening, not narrowing.

And then there's a deeper problem, which is the specification problem. Even if you could prove that a system satisfies some formal property, you have to write down what property you want. For a sorting algorithm that's easy. For "this AI will not do anything harmful to humanity," I have no idea how you would formalize that in a way that captures what we mean. The formal specification becomes the weak point. You end up proving the system does exactly what the spec says, and the spec may not say what you intended. That is more or less the whole alignment problem restated in logic, and formalizing it doesn't make it go away.

There's also the question of what you're verifying against. Modern AI systems are these enormous neural networks whose behavior emerges from training rather than from explicit design. You can't really prove theorems about what a trillion-parameter transformer will do on inputs it hasn't seen. You might be able to prove properties of a wrapper or a sandbox around it, but then the guarantee is about the sandbox, not about the intelligence inside, and a sufficiently clever system will find the edges of whatever cage you build if the cage is less intelligent than it is.

So my view is that it's good research to pursue. I would love for it to be further along. But if someone's plan for AGI safety hinges on having provably secure infrastructure in place before AGI arrives, I think that plan is going to be disappointed. I think we'll get AGI well before we get verified global infrastructure, and so we need approaches that work in a messy, unverified world. For me that means focusing on the cognitive architecture of the AGI itself, how it's raised and what it's taught to value, and decentralized governance, rather than betting on a mathematical shield that I don't believe will exist in time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the effort and limited scale of formal verification, but does not identify computational overhead as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: It does not mention quantum computing or homomorphic encryption.

r003.rationale: It says verified systems are tiny compared with the software ecosystem and that most deployed software remains unverified, conveying the lack of methods to prove security across most of the technology stack.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss countries adopting or forgoing costly infrastructure, or the competitive pressure between them.

astra-6.text:
Well, I’m sympathetic to the aspiration. If we could prove that important technological systems had the properties we wanted, that would be wonderful. My skepticism is about the distance between proving something about a formal model and securing the actual world.

A proof depends on assumptions. You specify the system, its environment, and what counts as safe, and then you prove that certain things follow. But real infrastructure interacts with people, physical devices, software nobody fully understands, and other systems that are changing. You can have a perfectly valid proof and still have a problem because one of your assumptions doesn’t hold.

With AGI, there’s an additional difficulty: we want systems that can learn new things, invent new representations, and operate in situations we didn’t anticipate. It’s much easier to prove properties of a narrowly constrained system than to prove that an open-ended intelligence will always do something compatible with human values. Even specifying what that means is a substantial unsolved problem.

So I’m not arguing against formal verification. I think it can be a valuable part of the toolkit. What I doubt is that we can extend it into a comprehensive, provably secure technological infrastructure on the timescale on which increasingly powerful AI is likely to arrive. That requires both mathematical advances and an enormous transformation of deployed systems. I wouldn’t want our approach to safety to depend on getting all of that done first.

r002.rationale: It says nothing about quantum computing or homomorphic encryption.

r003.rationale: It describes challenges from assumptions and changing real-world systems, but does not state that methods for proving security across most of the global technology stack are unknown.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss unilateral adoption, costs, or competitive pressure from countries that forgo security measures.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’m sympathetic to the goal. My doubt is about the gap between proving something about a formal model and securing a messy, evolving world. A proof holds given certain assumptions. But how do you establish that the hardware, the software, the people interacting with it, and the environment actually satisfy those assumptions? You can have a perfectly valid proof and still have left out the thing that causes the system to fail.

And with AGI, we’re talking about systems that learn, modify themselves, and encounter situations their designers didn’t anticipate. Specifying exactly what you want to prove becomes a substantial part of the problem. You don’t get a formal definition of beneficial behavior just by deciding to use formal methods.

I think we should use proofs wherever we can—for particular components, protocols, or constraints. But going from that to a provably secure technological infrastructure, on a timescale relevant to AGI development, strikes me as a very large leap. It’s an interesting research direction; I wouldn’t want our safety strategy to depend on achieving it in time.
